place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 大比 · 决赛 · 对马小宝
place.en: Chending Temple · The contest · The final · Against Ma Xiaobao

setup.zh: 决赛，在日落。对面是马小宝：一脸丹斑，练气五层，腰里挂着他家祖上那面照妖的铜镜：「你跪下，叫三声爷爷，我便不照了。」
setup.en: The final, at sunset. Facing you, Ma Xiaobao: pill-blotched, layer five, at his waist his forebears' demon-showing bronze mirror. "Kneel, call me grandpa three times, and I won't hold it up to you."

recap.zh: 决赛，马小宝的铜镜照向你的胸口；你头一回不藏，掌心接住了那道光，一掌三成——他在空中转了三圈，落进了泗水。观主把筑基丹放在你手里。
recap.en: In the final Ma Xiaobao's mirror went for your chest; for the first time you didn't hide, took its light in your palm, and struck with three-tenths — he turned three times in the air and landed in the Si. The abbot put the Foundation pill in your hand.

zh: 日落，决赛。对面，马小宝。一面照妖的铜镜。
en: Sunset, the final. Across from you, Ma Xiaobao. A demon-showing bronze mirror.
"Kneel, and call me grandpa three times."
"Bark like a dog, and you get a lick."

story.zh:
日头偏西，另一头打的是半决赛：马小宝对鲁泥鳅。鲁泥鳅上台前，从小满身边挤过去，压低了嗓子：「那面镜子，在我爹船舱里搁了一路。红布底下，半夜里自己亮过一回——冷的，像泗水底下的光。我爹说，那不是照妖的，是认东西的。」说完，他搓了搓手，上台去了。鲁泥鳅是渔户的儿子，水性好，身子滑，头一拳便钻到了马小宝腋下。马小宝这才摘下了铜镜。

小满站在台下，看得清清楚楚：那面镜子，不是一举就亮的。马小宝两手捧着它，脸上的斑「腾」地一红，一片一片鼓起来，像是有人往他身子里抽东西，抽出来，灌进镜子里——镜面这才亮了，一道黄光扑在鲁泥鳅脸上。鲁泥鳅「哎哟」一声，捂着眼睛倒退，嘴里直叫：「冷的！那光是冷的，往心口钻！」他退一步，马小宝又照一回，斑又红一回，喘得像风箱；照到第三回，鲁泥鳅一脚踩空，跌下了台。马小宝捧着镜子，站在那里喘了好一会儿，才喘匀。

小满心里慢慢地算了一笔账。昨天夜里，马小宝拿镜子照铺，没往里灌灵力，镜子上只有火光，木牌都烫成那样；今天灌了灵力，照上胸口，便不是烫一烫的事了。可那镜子是喝马小宝的灵力的：照一回，喝一口；一夜吞上去的两层，是虚的，经不起它喝几口。他想：那就让它喝。躲，一回一回地躲，让他一回一回地照，照到只剩最后一口——最后那一口，拿手接。

决赛在日落，太阳落到西边山头上的时候。另一头打上来的，是马小宝。

小满往台上走的时候，阿禾挤过来，塞给他半块烙饼，硬得像一块瓦：「垫垫肚子。空着肚子挨揍，更疼。」他把饼揣进怀里，贴着木牌，贴着那个饼角。

马小宝站在台上，腰里那面铜镜给落日一照，红得像一块烧透的炭。他冲台下团团一拱手，扯着嗓子道：「诸位！我这面镜子，是我家祖上拿三亩好地从一个游方道士手里换来的，能照妖，能退敌，能聚气，还能照见人心。今天，当着全外门，我拿它照一照——」他拿镜子一指小满，「——一个五行杂灵根，输了第一轮，平白冒出十块灵石，躲了师姐三十一剑，是人，是妖？」台下哄的一声，笑的，嚷的，起哄的，搅成一片。

马小宝又道：「沈小满。还是柴房那天的规矩——你跪下，叫三声爷爷，我便不照了，让你自己走下去。」台下有人起哄：「跪！跪！」一声接一声，起哄的人越来越多，喊到后来，竟有了节拍。便在这一片「跪」声里，人群当中忽然冒出一个嗓子，又尖又哑，破得像一面裂了的锣：「别跪——！」众人回头一看，是孙二狗。他下巴上贴着膏药，站在人堆里，比旁人高出半个头，脸涨得通红。四下里一愣，跟着便哄笑起来：「二狗！你一个输了的，喊什么！」孙二狗的脸红到了耳朵根，可他没有坐下，也没有缩回去，就那么直挺挺地站着。

小满站在台上，看着马小宝。他想起灶台上飞出去的那只碗，在半空里滴溜溜翻了两个筋斗，碗沿上白光一闪，他伸手去捞，差了一寸。他想起他娘蹲在地上，把碎片一片一片捡起来，用布包好，四个角系紧。他想起马小宝站在他家门口，手里捏着桂花糕，说：「学声狗叫，给你吃一口。」他想了想，开口道：「小宝哥。」马小宝道：「嗯？」小满说：「学声狗叫，给你舔一口。」

台下先是一愣，愣了足足一口气的工夫，跟着笑声便炸开了，从台下一路炸到了伙房，炸得老槐树上歇着的一群老鸹扑棱棱全飞了起来。马小宝那张斑斑点点的脸，先是红，再是紫，再是黑，最后变成了他爹的那种颜色——「完了」色。
story.en:
As the sun sank west, the semifinal was fought at the other end: Ma Xiaobao against Lu the Loach. Before going up, Lu squeezed past Xiaoman and said low: "That mirror sat in the hold of my father's boat all the way. Under the red cloth, one night, it lit up by itself — cold, like the light at the bottom of the Si. My father says it isn't for showing demons, it's for recognising things." Then he rubbed his hands and went up. Lu was a fisherman's son, slippery as his name, and his first punch ducked in under Ma Xiaobao's arm. Only then did Ma Xiaobao take off the mirror.

Below the stage Xiaoman saw it clearly: the mirror didn't light just by being raised. Ma Xiaobao held it in both hands, and the blotches on his face flared red and swelled patch by patch, as if something were being drawn out of him and poured into the mirror — only then did its face light, and a beam of yellow light hit Lu in the face. Lu yelped and staggered back clutching his eyes: "Cold! That light's cold — it goes for your heart!" He backed a step; Ma Xiaobao lit it again, the blotches flared again, and he wheezed like a bellows; at the third flash Lu missed his footing and fell off the stage. Ma Xiaobao stood holding the mirror, panting a long while before he got his breath.

Xiaoman worked out a sum, slowly. Last night Ma Xiaobao had swept the bunks with that mirror without pouring any power into it — nothing on it but firelight, and still the token had burned like that; today, with power poured in, landing on his chest, it wouldn't stop at burning. But the mirror drank Ma Xiaobao's power: one flash, one mouthful; and two layers swallowed in a night were hollow, they couldn't stand many mouthfuls. Then let it drink, he thought. Dodge, and dodge again, and let him flash it again and again, till he's down to the last mouthful — and that last one, take in the hand.

The final was at sunset, when the sun sat on the western hills. Coming up from the other side was Ma Xiaobao.

As Xiaoman went up to the stage, A He squeezed over and pushed half a flatbread at him, hard as a roof tile: "Line your stomach. A beating on an empty stomach hurts more." He tucked it into his coat, against the token, against that corner of flatbread.

Ma Xiaobao stood on the stage, the bronze mirror at his waist red in the setting sun like a coal burned through. He cupped his fists all round and bawled: "Everyone! This mirror my forebears traded three good acres for, from a wandering Taoist — it shows demons, repels enemies, gathers qi, and shows the heart. Today, before the whole outer court, I'll hold it up to —" he pointed it at Xiaoman, "— a mixed-root boy who lost his first round, suddenly turned up with ten stones, and dodged a senior's sword thirty-one times. Man, or demon?" The crowd erupted — laughing, shouting, egging on, all in a jumble.

"Shen Xiaoman," said Ma Xiaobao, "same rule as the woodshed — kneel, call me grandpa three times, and I won't hold it up; I'll let you walk down yourself." Someone below started up: "Kneel! Kneel!" Again and again, more and more of them, till it took on a beat. And in the middle of the chanting a voice rose from the crowd, shrill and hoarse, cracked like a split gong: "Don't kneel —!" Everyone turned: Sun Ergou, a plaster on his chin, half a head above the crowd, face flushed dark. A pause, then laughter: "Ergou! You lost, what are you yelling for!" Sun Ergou went red to the ears, but he didn't sit down and he didn't shrink back; he just stood there, straight.

Xiaoman stood on the stage and looked at Ma Xiaobao. He remembered the bowl flying off the stove, turning two somersaults in the air, a flash of white on its rim, his hand reaching and missing by an inch. He remembered his mother crouched on the floor picking up the pieces one by one, wrapping them in cloth, tying the four corners. He remembered Ma Xiaobao at their door with an osmanthus cake: "Bark like a dog and you get a bite." He thought, and said: "Brother Xiaobao." "Hm?" "Bark like a dog," said Xiaoman, "and you get a lick."

For a moment the crowd was stunned — a full breath — and then the laughter exploded, from the stage to the kitchen, and the crows in the old pagoda tree went flapping up all together. Ma Xiaobao's blotched face went red, then purple, then black, and at last his father's colour — the colour of done for.

label.en: Bark like a dog, and you get a lick

exits.means: answers Ma Xiaobao's taunt and fights him for the pill

withdrawn.zh: 马小宝的铜镜又亮了，他笑得更开心了。——再来。
withdrawn.en: Ma Xiaobao's mirror flashes again, and he smiles even wider. — Again.

story.zh:
他一把扯下腰里的铜镜，两手捧起来，脸上的斑「腾」地红了。镜面一亮，一道黄光扑向小满的腿。小满往旁边一跳，那道光打在青石板上，石缝里的草登时白了一片。马小宝又照，他又跳；又照，他又滚。台下起先笑他躲得难看，笑到第四回，便没人笑了：马小宝每照一回，脸上的斑便鼓一回，红一回，捧镜子的手一回比一回抖，喘得像一只风箱。他站住了，咬着牙道：「躲？你就会躲？」小满道：「小宝哥，镜子是你家的，照多了，费油。」

马小宝咬着牙，把身子里剩下的那一口，全灌进了镜子里。镜面亮得发白，一道黄光，不奔腿，不奔面门，直奔小满的胸口。

那一霎，小满胸口的木牌烫得像一块烧红的铁。这一道，他等了五道。他没有躲。他把一只手抬到了胸前，掌心朝外，把那一线封了三十几天的火，头一回，扒开了。

那一道黄光撞在他掌心前三寸的地方，便像一滴水落进了一口很大很大的水缸里，没了，连个响也没有。台下的人什么也没看清，只当马小宝的镜子亮了一亮，便没有下文了，倒像一盏灯芯受了潮的油灯，扑哧一声，灭了——灯油，早叫他自己照干了。

马小宝举着铜镜，傻站在台上。他把镜子翻过来看看，又翻过去看看，使劲拍了两下，好像那镜子是一只不肯下蛋的鸡。小满往前走了一步：「小宝哥。九月初十，公中，一块灵石。十月初一，一块。冬月初一，两块。腊月初一，两块——冬月初一许的免交，未兑。」又往前走了一步：「十月十二，柴房，二十三下。」再往前走了一步，已到了马小宝跟前：「利息，另算。」

一掌拍出。这一掌，他只出了三成，七成留在手里——三成，打得倒，打不死，旁人看了，只当马小宝自己站不稳。可他算漏了一样：马小宝一夜吞下去的三瓶丹，丹毒淤在经脉里，灵力本来就是虚的，又叫那面镜子喝去了大半，像一口破缸，外头看着满，底下全是裂缝。三成的力道拍上去，马小宝登时飞了出去，在半空里滴溜溜转了三个圈，姿态倒是颇为优美，越过了台子，越过了人群，越过了外门的院墙，远远地只听得「扑通」一声，落进了泗水里。

山脚下泗水边，马三那条船还泊着，那面「仙途无量」的旗还插着。马三在船上从早等到日落，等来的是他儿子从天而降，「扑通」一声，正落在船头前三尺，溅了他一身。他把儿子从腊月的泗水里拎上来，拎上来一看，嘴里还叼着一根水草。那面旗，后来让风吹进了泗水，顺水漂走了。

台上台下三百多人，一个声音也没有。褚先生站在人群最后头，一只手捋着山羊胡子，捋到一半，停在半空。隔了好一会儿，才有一个声音怯生生地道：「……他……他那是……反噬了吧？」这一声像是给众人打开了一扇门：「对对对，反噬！吃丹吃坏了！」「一夜吞了三瓶丹，灵力是虚的！」「褚先生讲过的，轻则退三层，重则废！」「我就说他脸上那些斑不对劲！」越说越信，越信越觉得自己早就看出来了。褚先生的山羊胡子终于落了下来，他咳了一声，沉着脸道：「丹药之道，贪多必失。诸位引以为戒。」说罢转身走了，走的时候，回头看了小满一眼。

没有人问沈小满练气几层。只有两个人不这么觉得。一个是台北面竹椅上的观主玄沉子，他从头到尾没动过，这时候却轻轻「嗯」了一声。另一个是山门台阶上的瞿老，他背对着演武场，一直在扫地；马小宝飞过院墙的那一刻，他的扫帚停了，停在那一级台阶上。那一级台阶，他扫了五十年，这一天，没有扫完。

小满胸口的木牌凉了下来，一个很困的声音在他耳朵里道：「……三成？」他小声道：「嗯。」那声音打了个哈欠：「……下回用两成。泗水离这儿，太近了。」

头名，筑基丹一枚。照观里的老例，头名的名字要当着全外门的面，由周衡写进那本蓝布面的名录。周衡蘸饱了墨，一笔一画地写下「沈小满」三个字，写得比平时慢，写完了，拿嘴吹了吹，又把名录往前翻了几十页，翻到划了一道的那一页，看了一眼，才又翻回来。跟着他掏出自己那本账簿，在腊月初八那一行底下添了三行：**赏灵石十块，沈小满，巡夜有功。复试用尽。头名得丹。**顿了一顿，又添了三个字：**账平了。**人群后头一阵骚动，马小宝回来了，裹着他爹的棉袍，头发上结着冰碴子，湿淋淋地一路走，一路滴水，滴到五行台跟前，看见观主正把一只玉盒子往沈小满手里放，站住了，张了张嘴，打了一个惊天动地的喷嚏。

那玉盒子玉色青白，盒盖上贴着一道封条，封条上盖着沉鼎观的大印。玄沉子把它放在小满手里，手却没有马上松开，看着他，道：「五行杂灵根？」小满道：「是。」玄沉子道：「练气二层？」小满道：「……是。」玄沉子笑了，笑得很温和，说话却照旧只说半句：「沉鼎秘境里，有一间石室。三百年，没人进去过……」他没说完，低头看了一眼小满的草鞋，拍了拍他的肩膀，转身走了。小满捧着玉盒站在那里，后背上的汗，一下子全冒了出来。

他捧着玉盒走下五行台的时候，往山门那边望了一眼。瞿老站在台阶上，拄着扫帚，也在看。可瞿老看的不是他，是他手里那只玉盒子。那一眼很长，长得不像是在看一只盒子，倒像是在看一件很多年以前的旧事。然后瞿老转过身去，扫地了。

台阶底下，褚先生在等他。人都往伙房那边散了，老先生一个人站在那里，冲他伸出两根指头：「腕子。」小满把腕子递过去，心里咚咚地跳，灶膛里那一线火，一层灰，又一层灰，死死地封着。褚先生搭了很久，久到山门那边瞿老的扫帚又响了起来。他松了手，道：「脉上是二层。」捋了一下山羊胡子，转身走了，走出去三步，头也不回，又补了一句：「掌上不是。」
story.en:
He tore the bronze mirror from his waist and held it up in both hands, and the blotches on his face flared red. Its face lit, and a beam of yellow light went for Xiaoman's legs. Xiaoman hopped aside; the light struck the bluestone and the grass in the crack went white at once. Ma Xiaobao flashed again; he hopped again; again, and he rolled. At first the crowd laughed at how badly he dodged; by the fourth time no one was laughing: every flash, the blotches on Ma Xiaobao's face swelled and flared, the hands holding the mirror shook worse, and he wheezed like a bellows. He stopped and said through his teeth: "Dodge? Is that all you can do?" "Brother Xiaobao," said Xiaoman, "it's your family's mirror. Use it too much and it burns the oil."

Teeth clenched, Ma Xiaobao poured the last mouthful he had into the mirror. Its face blazed white, and a beam of yellow light went not for his legs, not for his face, but straight for Xiaoman's chest.

In that instant the token on Xiaoman's chest burned like red-hot iron. This beam he had waited five beams for. He didn't dodge. He raised one hand before his chest, palm out, and raked open, for the first time, the one thread of fire he had kept banked for thirty-odd days.

The yellow beam struck three inches before his palm and was gone, like a drop of water falling into a very, very big vat — not even a sound. The crowd saw nothing; they only saw Ma Xiaobao's mirror flash and then nothing more, like an oil lamp with a damp wick: pfft, out — its oil long since burned dry by his own hand.

Ma Xiaobao stood there with the mirror up, dumbfounded. He turned it over and back again and slapped it twice, as if it were a hen that wouldn't lay. Xiaoman stepped forward: "Brother Xiaobao. Tenth of the ninth month, common fund, one stone. First of the tenth month, one. First of the eleventh, two. First of the twelfth, two — and the waiver you promised on the first of the eleventh, not honoured." Another step: "Twelfth of the tenth month, the woodshed, twenty-three blows." Another step, and he stood before Ma Xiaobao: "Interest, separately."

One palm. He put out only three-tenths and kept seven in his hand — three-tenths, enough to knock him down and not kill him, so that onlookers would think Ma Xiaobao just lost his footing. But he'd missed one thing in his sums: the three bottles Ma Xiaobao had swallowed in one night had clogged his meridians with poison; his power was hollow to begin with, and the mirror had drunk most of it — a cracked vat, full to look at and split all through underneath. The three-tenths landed and Ma Xiaobao flew — turned three somersaults in the air, rather gracefully, over the stage, over the crowd, over the outer court's wall, and from far off came a single splash, into the Si.

Down at the foot of the mountain, Ma San's boat was still moored, the Boundless on the Immortal Road banner still flying. Ma San had waited in the boat from morning to sunset, and what came was his son out of the sky — splash — three feet in front of the bow, drenching him. He hauled his son out of the twelfth-month Si, and when he had him up there was waterweed in his mouth. That banner the wind later blew into the Si, and it floated away downstream.

Three hundred-odd people on and off the stage, and not a sound. At the very back, Master Chu stood with a hand on his goatee, stopped halfway down. After a long while a timid voice said: "…He… that was… backlash, wasn't it?" That opened a door: "Yes, yes, backlash! Ate too many pills!" "Three bottles in one night — his power's hollow!" "Master Chu told us — at best you drop three layers, at worst you're crippled!" "I knew those blotches weren't right!" The more they said it the more they believed it, and the more they believed it the surer they were they'd seen it all along. Master Chu's goatee finally came down. He coughed, and said sternly: "In the way of pills, greed brings loss. Take warning, all of you." He turned to go, and going, looked back once at Xiaoman.

Nobody asked what layer Shen Xiaoman was at. Only two people didn't think so. One was the abbot, Xuanchenzi, on his bamboo chair north of the stage; he hadn't moved from first to last, but now he said softly, "Mm." The other was Elder Qu on the steps at the gate, his back to the ground, sweeping all along; the moment Ma Xiaobao flew over the wall, his broom stopped, stopped on that one step. The step he had swept for fifty years went unfinished that day.

The token on Xiaoman's chest cooled, and a very sleepy voice said in his ear: "…Three-tenths?" "Mm," he whispered. The voice yawned: "…Use two next time. The Si's too close."

First place: one Foundation pill. By temple custom the winner's name was written into the blue register by Zhou Heng before the whole outer court. Zhou Heng dipped his brush full and wrote the three characters Shen Xiaoman stroke by stroke, slower than usual, blew on them, then turned back dozens of pages to the one with the stroke through it, looked, and turned forward again. Then he took out his own ledger and added three lines under the eighth of the twelfth month: **Ten stones, Shen Xiaoman, merit on night watch. Spent on the second trial. First place, pill won.** A pause, and three more words: **Accounts balanced.** A stir at the back of the crowd: Ma Xiaobao was back, wrapped in his father's padded gown, ice in his hair, dripping all the way; he dripped up to the platform, saw the abbot placing a jade box in Shen Xiaoman's hands, stopped, opened his mouth, and let out an earth-shaking sneeze.

The jade box was bluish-white, a seal strip across its lid stamped with the temple's great seal. Xuanchenzi laid it in Xiaoman's hands but didn't let go at once. He looked at him: "Five-element mixed roots?" "Yes." "Qi Refining, layer two?" "…Yes." Xuanchenzi smiled, very mildly, and as always said only half: "In the Chending hidden realm there is a stone chamber. For three hundred years, no one has gone in…" He didn't finish; he glanced down at Xiaoman's straw sandals, patted his shoulder, and walked away. Xiaoman stood holding the box, and the sweat broke out all down his back.

As he carried the box down off the platform he looked toward the gate. Elder Qu stood on the steps leaning on his broom, looking too. But he wasn't looking at Xiaoman; he was looking at the jade box in his hands. A long look, not like looking at a box, more like looking at something that happened many years ago. Then he turned away and swept.

At the foot of the steps Master Chu was waiting for him. Everyone had drifted off toward the kitchen; the old teacher stood there alone and held out two fingers: "Your wrist." Xiaoman gave it, his heart thudding, the one thread of fire in his stove banked hard under ash on ash. Chu held it a long time, so long that over at the gate Elder Qu's broom began to sweep again. He let go: "The pulse says layer two." He stroked his goatee, turned and walked away, and three steps on, without looking back, added: "The palm doesn't."
